claim: The diffusion coefficient for free GFP in the Arabidopsis root was 6.33 ± 0.37 μm²/s (n = 34 for different cells, including vascular, endodermal, and QC cells).
source: In the Arabidopsis root, the resulting DC for free GFP was 6.33 ± 0.37 μm2/s (n = 34 for different cells, including vascular, endodermal, and QC cells) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements using RICS analysis on 35S:GFP in Arabidopsis roots, with sample size and standard error provided.

claim: Similar diffusion coefficients for free GFP were obtained using two different confocal microscopes (Zeiss 780 and Zeiss 710).
source: We obtained similar diffusion coefficients using two different confocal microscopes (Zeiss 780 and Zeiss 710).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental validation across two different instruments.

claim: SHR moves at a rate of 2.45 ± 0.26 μm²/s (n = 40) within a population of vascular and endodermal cells.
source: Our RICS analysis showed that SHR moves at a rate of 2.45 ± 0.26 μm2/s (n = 40) and 1.73 ± 0.15 µm2/s (n = 16) within a population of vascular and endodermal cells and vascular and QC cells, respectively (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RICS measurements on SHR:SHR-GFP in shr2 complemented line.

claim: SHR moves at a rate of 1.73 ± 0.15 µm²/s (n = 16) within a population of vascular and QC cells.
source: Our RICS analysis showed that SHR moves at a rate of 2.45 ± 0.26 μm2/s (n = 40) and 1.73 ± 0.15 µm2/s (n = 16) within a population of vascular and endodermal cells and vascular and QC cells, respectively (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RICS measurements on SHR:SHR-GFP in shr2 complemented line.

claim: In a population of only endodermal cells, SHR moves at a significantly slower rate (1.29 ± 0.14 μm²/s n = 19, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p = 0.0303).
source: Notably, in a population of only endodermal cells, SHR moves at a significantly slower rate (1.29 ± 0.14 μm2/s n = 19, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p = 0.0303) (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RICS measurements with statistical analysis showing significant difference.

claim: SHR diffusion in populations of only endodermal cells in the SCRi line was similar to that in populations of vascular and endodermal cells (2.40 ± 0.29 μm²/s, n = 14, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p = 0.9337).
source: In this line, in which the levels of SCR are reduced, SHR diffusion in populations of only endodermal cells was similar to that in populations of vascular and endodermal cells (2.40 ± 0.29 μm2/s, n = 14, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p = 0.9337) (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RICS measurements in SCRi background with statistical analysis.

claim: RICS data are in agreement with genetic and molecular data that show SHR movement is restricted by SCR.
source: Overall, our RICS data are in agreement with genetic and molecular data that show SHR movement is restricted by SCR (Heidstra et al., 2004; Cui et al., 2007; Long et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental RICS data and references to previous genetic and molecular studies.

claim: 35S:GFP had a Movement Index (MI) of 0.71 ± 0.07 (n = 15).
source: As a positive control, we acquired pCF data for 35SGFP, which had a MI = 0.71 ± 0.07 (n = 15).
evidence: The claim is supported by pCF measurements on 35S:GFP as a positive control.

claim: TMO5:3xGFP had a Movement Index (MI) of 0.26 ± 0.05 (n = 19).
source: To this end, we drove the 3xGFP using a root vasculature promoter (TMO5:3xGFP, Schlereth et al., 2010) which had a MI = 0.26 ± 0.05 (n = 19) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by pCF measurements on TMO5:3xGFP as a negative control.

claim: SHR moves from the vasculature to the endodermis (MI = 0.58 ± 0.03, n = 20, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p = 0.6356).
source: We found that SHR moves from the vasculature to the endodermis (MI = 0.58 ± 0.03, n = 20, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p = 0.6356), consistent with previous experimental data (Helariutta et al., 2000; Nakajima et al., 2001) (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by pCF measurements with statistical analysis and references to previous studies.

claim: From the endodermis back to the vasculature, the MI of SHR was significantly lower than the MI of free GFP (MI = 0.36 ± 0.07, n = 20, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p = 0.0368).
source: However, from the endodermis back to the vasculature, the MI of SHR was significantly lower than the MI of free GFP (MI = 0.36 ± 0.07, n = 20, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p = 0.0368) and not significantly different from the MI of the 3xGFP (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p = 0.5974), suggesting that SHR is unable to move back to the vasculature (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by pCF measurements with statistical analysis comparing to controls.

claim: SHR moves bidirectionally between the endodermis and cortex, as the MI is not significantly different from that of free GFP (MI = 0.61 ± 0.06 from endodermis to cortex, MI = 0.53 ± 0.06 from cortex to endodermis, n = 20, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p = 0.9524 and p = 0.3909 respectively).
source: In addition, we found that SHR moves bidirectionally between the endodermis and cortex, as the MI is not significantly different from that of free GFP (MI = 0.61 ± 0.06 from endodermis to cortex, MI = 0.53 ± 0.06 from cortex to endodermis, n = 20, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p = 0.9524 and p = 0.3909 respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by pCF measurements with statistical analysis in both directions.

claim: In the SCRi line, SHR movement from the vasculature to the endodermis had a MI = 0.66 ± 0.07 (n = 14).
source: We not only observed SHR movement from the vasculature to the endodermis with a MI = 0.66 ± 0.07 (n = 14) but also from the endodermis back to the vasculature with a MI = 0.78 ± 0.09 (n = 14) (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by pCF measurements in SCRi background.

claim: In the SCRi line, SHR movement from the endodermis back to the vasculature had a MI = 0.78 ± 0.09 (n = 14).
source: We not only observed SHR movement from the vasculature to the endodermis with a MI = 0.66 ± 0.07 (n = 14) but also from the endodermis back to the vasculature with a MI = 0.78 ± 0.09 (n = 14) (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by pCF measurements in SCRi background.

claim: The MI for SHR:SHR-GFP in SCRi in both directions is not significantly different from the MI for 35S:GFP (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p = 0.9553 for endo to vasc, p = 0.9999 for vasc to endo), suggesting that movement is unrestricted in both directions.
source: Since the MI for SHR:SHR-GFP in SCRi in both directions is not significantly different from the MI for 35S:GFP (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p = 0.9553 for endo to vasc, p = 0.9999 for vasc to endo) it suggests that movement is unrestricted in both directions (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by pCF measurements with statistical analysis and inference about unrestricted movement.

claim: In the SCRi line, SHR is still able to move bidirectionally between the endodermis and cortex (MI = 0.61 ± 0.05 from endodermis to cortex, MI = 0.59 ± 0.07 from cortex to endodermis, n = 17, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p = 0.9997 and p = 0.5510 respectively).
source: Similarly, we found that SHR is still able to move bidirectionally between the endodermis and cortex (MI = 0.61 ± 0.05 from endodermis to cortex, MI = 0.59 ± 0.07 from cortex to endodermis, n = 17, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p = 0.9997 and p = 0.5510 respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by pCF measurements in SCRi background with statistical analysis.

claim: The presence of SCR prevents SHR movement specifically from the endodermis back to the vasculature while it does not affect the movement between the endodermis and cortex.
source: These results suggest that the presence of SCR prevents SHR movement specifically from the endodermis back to the vasculature while it does not affect the movement between the endodermis and cortex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from pCF measurements comparing wild type and SCRi lines.

claim: SCR does not move between the endodermis and the cortex, as the MI in either direction is significantly lower than that of 35S:GFP (MI = 0.31 ± 0.08 from endodermis to cortex, MI = 0.31 ± 0.07 from cortex to endodermis, n = 14, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p = 0.0236 and p = 0.0054 respectively).
source: Our results show that SCR does not move between the endodermis and the cortex, as the MI in either direction is significantly lower than that of 35S:GFP (MI = 0.31 ± 0.08 from endodermis to cortex, MI = 0.31 ± 0.07 from cortex to endodermis, n = 14, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p = 0.0236 and p = 0.0054 respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by pCF measurements on SCR:SCR-GFP with statistical analysis.

claim: SHR exists primarily as a monomer in the vasculature, with SHR homodimer formation at only 2.6% ± 0.3%.
source: Our results indicated that SHR exists primarily as a monomer in the vasculature, given that SHR homodimer formation was only 2.6% ± 0.3% in these cells (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by N&B analysis on SHR:SHR-GFP in vascular cells.

claim: SHR monomeric proteins are observed in both the nuclei and in the cytoplasm of vasculature cells.
source: Notably, SHR monomeric proteins are observed in both the nuclei and in the cytoplasm of vasculature cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by N&B analysis observations.

claim: In the nuclei of the endodermis, there are significantly more SHR homodimers present (7.5% ± 0.9% homodimer, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p<0.0001).
source: By contrast, in the nuclei of the endodermis, there are significantly more SHR homodimers present (7.5% ± 0.9% homodimer, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p<0.0001) (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by N&B analysis with statistical comparison to vascular cells.

claim: In the endodermis, SHR is present at very low levels outside of the nuclei.
source: Moreover, in the endodermis SHR is present at very low levels outside of the nuclei (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by N&B analysis observations.

claim: In the SCRi line, SHR is mainly found as a monomer in the endodermis (1.9% ± 0.4% homodimer, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p = 0.2546), indicating that SCR influences the oligomeric composition of SHR.
source: Therefore, we performed N&B on SHR:SHR-GFP in the SCRi line and observed that SHR is mainly found as a monomer in the endodermis (1.9% ± 0.4% homodimer, Wilcoxon with Steel-Dwass, p = 0.2546), indicating that SCR influences the oligomeric composition of SHR (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by N&B analysis in SCRi background with statistical analysis and inference about SCR's influence.

claim: SCR:SCR-mCherry line had mostly monomers with 4.7% ± 0.5% of homodimers.
source: In the SCR:SCR-mCherry line, we detected mostly monomers with 4.7% ± 0.5% of homodimers (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by N&B analysis on SCR:SCR-mCherry.

claim: The SCR:SCR-GFP line had 5.4% ± 0.7% of homodimers, which is similar to the SCR:SCR-mCherry line.
source: We found that the SCR:SCR-GFP line had 5.4% ± 0.7% of homodimers, which is similar to the SCR:SCR-mCherry line (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by N&B analysis on SCR:SCR-GFP with comparison to mCherry-tagged version.

claim: Both the monomer and the homodimer of SHR bind the monomer of SCR, suggesting that SHR and SCR bind with a 1:1 and 2:1 stoichiometry.
source: We found that both the monomer and the homodimer of SHR bind the monomer of SCR, suggesting that SHR and SCR bind with a 1:1 and 2:1 stoichiometry (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-N&B analysis on SHR:SHR-GFP/SCR:SCR-mCherry line.

claim: 84.8% ± 1.6% of the SHR-SCR complexes have 1:1 stoichiometry while 15.2% ± 1.6% have 2:1 stoichiometry.
source: Additionally, we determined that 84.8% ± 1.6% of the SHR-SCR complexes have 1:1 stoichiometry while 15.2% ± 1.6% have 2:1 stoichiometry (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-N&B analysis quantifying complex stoichiometry.

claim: The homodimer of SCR does not seem to be part of the SHR-SCR complex.
source: We were not able to detect any complexes that contain the homodimer of SCR.
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-N&B analysis results.

claim: The rate of movement of SHR from the vasculature to the endodermis (a1) and from the endodermis to the vasculature (a2) are both highly influential parameters in the mathematical model.
source: Using this measure, we found that the rate of movement of SHR from the vasculature to the endodermis (a1) and from the endodermis to the vasculature (a2) are both highly influential parameters (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Sobol sensitivity analysis of the mathematical model.

claim: SHR movement is a key component of the model that greatly influences the dynamics of SHR in the endodermis.
source: Thus, this suggests that SHR movement is a key component of the model that greatly influences the dynamics of SHR in the endodermis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the sensitivity analysis results.

claim: The mathematical model predicts that SHR reaches a steady state in the vasculature and endodermis in a matter of minutes.
source: Our mathematical model predicts that SHR reaches a steady state in the vasculature and endodermis in a matter of minutes.
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical model simulations.

claim: The levels of SCR increase greatly in the first 3 hr, which is supported by data that show that SCR expression in a SHR inducible system is significant after 3 hr.
source: The levels of SCR increase greatly in the first 3 hr, which is supported by data that show that SCR expression in a SHR inducible system is significant after 3 hr (Sozzani et al, 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical model simulations and supported by cited experimental data.

claim: While the 1:1 SHR-SCR complex increases greatly in the first 3 hr, the 2:1 complex does not form until after 9 hr.
source: While the 1:1 SHR-SCR complex increases greatly in the first 3 hr, the 2:1 complex does not form until after 9 hr.
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical model simulations.

claim: The SHR homodimer does not form until about 9 hr into the simulation.
source: This is because the SHR homodimer does not form until about 9 hr into the simulation (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical model simulations.

claim: The entire system reaches a steady-state between 18 and 24 hr.
source: Finally, the entire system reaches a steady-state between 18 and 24 hr (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical model simulations.

claim: Cell division occurs once SCR and the SHR-SCR complexes reach their steady state values.
source: This suggests that cell division occurs once SCR and the SHR-SCR complexes reach their steady state values.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mathematical model results.

claim: In the SCRi model, at lower levels of SCR, the steady-state value of the 1:1 SHR-SCR complex is reduced by half.
source: At these lower levels of SCR, we observe that the steady-state value of the 1:1 SHR-SCR complex is reduced by half (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical model simulations of SCRi conditions.

claim: In the SCRi model, SHR homodimers do not form as seen in the N&B analysis.
source: In addition, we observe that SHR homodimers do not form as seen in the N&B analysis (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical model simulations consistent with experimental N&B data.

claim: Since SHR homodimers do not form in the SCRi model, the 2:1 SHR-SCR complex does not exist.
source: Since SHR homodimers do not form, the 2:1 SHR-SCR complex does not exist (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical model simulations and logical inference.

claim: The extra layer in the SCRi line could form due to a reduction in the levels of the SHR-SCR complex.
source: These results suggest that the extra layer in the SCRi line could form due to a reduction in the levels of the SHR-SCR complex.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on model results suggesting a possible mechanism.

claim: There are still other unknown factors that could contribute to the formation of the extra layer in the SCRi line.
source: However, there are still other unknown factors that could contribute to the formation of the extra layer.
evidence: The claim acknowledges limitations and unknown factors.

claim: Trafficking along the radial axis is normally unidirectional - SHR moves from the vasculature to the endodermis, and not in the opposite direction.
source: Trafficking along the radial axis is normally unidirectional - SHR moves from the vasculature to the endodermis, and not in the opposite direction (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by pCF analysis results.

claim: In the absence of SCR, SHR trafficking is bidirectional.
source: In the absence of SCR, SHR trafficking is bidirectional.
evidence: The claim is supported by pCF analysis in SCRi background.

claim: The DC of SHR in the endodermis increases significantly in the absence of SCR as compared to wild type, indicating that removal of SCR affects the diffusive behavior of SHR.
source: In agreement with the pCF results, our RICS data showed that the DC of SHR in the endodermis increases significantly in the absence of SCR as compared to wild type, indicating that removal of SCR affects the diffusive behavior of SHR.
evidence: The claim is supported by RICS measurements comparing wild type and SCRi, with inference about SCR's effect.

claim: SCR, which is present only in the endodermis, spatially restricts SHR movement.
source: Taken together, these results provide further evidence that SCR, which is present only in the endodermis, spatially restricts SHR movement.
evidence: The claim is inferred from combined RICS and pCF results.

claim: The DC measurements of SHR in both the shr2 complemented line and SCRi are significantly lower than those of freely-moving 35S:GFP (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.0001).
source: The DC measurements of SHR in both the shr2 complemented line and SCRi are significantly lower than those of freely-moving 35S:GFP (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.0001) (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RICS measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: The change in DC is not attributable to the molecular weight of SHR.
source: However, since the DC of SHR is three-fold smaller than the DC of 35S:GFP, and the DC is inversely proportional to the cube root of the molecular weight of the protein (Young et al., 1980), the change in DC is not attributable to the molecular weight of SHR (~60 kDa).
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical calculations using known relationships between DC and molecular weight, with citation.

claim: If the change in DC were due to molecular weight, the molecular weight of SHR would have to be 27-fold higher than that of GFP, or approximately 729 kDa.
source: If it were, then the molecular weight of SHR would have to be 27-fold higher than that of GFP, or approximately 729 kDa (Prendergast and Manni, 1978).
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical calculations with citation.

claim: The decrease in the DC of SHR relative to 35S:GFP, in addition to the pCF analysis which shows unidirectional movement, suggests an active regulation of SHR movement.
source: Further, the decrease in the DC of SHR relative to 35S:GFP, in addition to the pCF analysis which shows unidirectional movement, suggests an active regulation of SHR movement, which is in agreement with previous data (Gallagher et al., 2004; Sena et al., 2004; Gallagher and Benfey, 2009).
evidence: The claim is inferred from combined RICS and pCF data, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SHR is transcribed in the vasculature.
source: SHR is transcribed in the vasculature (Helariutta et al., 2000; Nakajima et al., 2001), and then the protein moves to the adjacent cell layer where it is retained in the nuclei of the Quiescent Center (QC), Cortex/Endodermis Initials (CEI) and endodermis (Nakajima et al., 2001; Gallagher et al., 2004; Gallagher and Benfey, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SHR protein moves to the adjacent cell layer where it is retained in the nuclei of the Quiescent Center (QC), Cortex/Endodermis Initials (CEI) and endodermis.
source: SHR is transcribed in the vasculature (Helariutta et al., 2000; Nakajima et al., 2001), and then the protein moves to the adjacent cell layer where it is retained in the nuclei of the Quiescent Center (QC), Cortex/Endodermis Initials (CEI) and endodermis (Nakajima et al., 2001; Gallagher et al., 2004; Gallagher and Benfey, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SHR activates the expression of the downstream transcription factor SCR.
source: In these cells, SHR activates the expression of the downstream transcription factor SCR (Helariutta et al., 2000; Levesque et al., 2006; Cui et al., 2007; Sozzani et al., 2010), which, as shown by yeast two hybrid experiments, interacts with SHR and prevents further SHR movement (Heidstra et al., 2004; Cui et al., 2007; Long et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SCR interacts with SHR and prevents further SHR movement, as shown by yeast two hybrid experiments.
source: In these cells, SHR activates the expression of the downstream transcription factor SCR (Helariutta et al., 2000; Levesque et al., 2006; Cui et al., 2007; Sozzani et al., 2010), which, as shown by yeast two hybrid experiments, interacts with SHR and prevents further SHR movement (Heidstra et al., 2004; Cui et al., 2007; Long et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies including yeast two hybrid experiments.

claim: The SHR-SCR mediated gene regulatory network (GRN) is a well-characterized developmental pathway that controls ground tissue patterning and endodermal cell fate specification.
source: In the Arabidopsis root, the SHORTROOT-SCARECROW (SHR-SCR) mediated gene regulatory network (GRN) is a well-characterized developmental pathway that controls ground tissue patterning and endodermal cell fate specification (Levesque et al., 2006; Cui et al., 2007; Sozzani et al., 2010; Cruz-Ramırez et al., 2012; Long et al., 2015; Moreno-Risueno et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 3xGFP was shown to restrict free GFP movement in roots.
source: As a negative control we used 3xGFP, which was shown to restrict free GFP movement in roots (Kim et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: A 60% reduction of SCR is required to produce the mutant layer in the SCRi line.
source: It has been shown that the mutant layer in the SCRi line occurs when the concentration of SCR drops to 60% of WT levels (Cui et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The SHR:SHR-GFP translational fusion complements the shr2 mutant phenotype.
source: To this end, we used a SHR:SHR-GFP translational fusion, which complements the shr2 mutant phenotype (SHR:SHR-GFP in shr2) (Nakajima et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: RICS and pCF introduce a spatial component that can determine whether slow movement is due to a binding interaction or slow diffusion, which FRAP and single-point FCS cannot do.
source: Moreover, RICS and pCF introduce a spatial component that can determine whether slow movement is due to a binding interaction or slow diffusion, which FRAP and single-point FCS cannot do.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the capabilities of different techniques.

claim: Scanning FCS methods are robust against cell movement and other artifacts that could bias measurements taken with other single-point methods.
source: Thus, these scanning FCS methods are robust against cell movement and other artifacts that could bias measurements taken with other single-point methods.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the advantages of scanning FCS methods.

claim: The DC is inversely proportional to the cube root of the molecular weight of the protein.
source: However, since the DC of SHR is three-fold smaller than the DC of 35S:GFP, and the DC is inversely proportional to the cube root of the molecular weight of the protein (Young et al., 1980), the change in DC is not attributable to the molecular weight of SHR (~60 kDa).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge with citation.

claim: Some transcription factors must form higher order complexes in order to function.
source: Stoichiometry is an important feature of protein complexes, as some transcription factors must form higher order complexes in order to function (Nakashima et al., 2012; Sornaraj et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge with citations.

claim: The intercellular movement of transcription factors and the spatio-temporal control of protein complex formation regulate many processes including cell fate specification in plants.
source: In plants, the intercellular movement of transcription factors and the spatio-temporal control of protein complex formation regulate many processes including cell fate specification.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Many of the signaling mechanisms regulating development utilize mobile signals that cross cell boundaries.
source: Many of the signaling mechanisms regulating development utilize mobile signals that cross cell boundaries (Koizumi et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011; Gallagher et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge with citations.

claim: During development, multicellular organisms must coordinate patterning, maintenance, and growth of different cell types through complex spatio-temporal signaling mechanisms.
source: During development, multicellular organisms must coordinate patterning, maintenance, and growth of different cell types. This dynamic coordination is achieved through complex spatio-temporal signaling mechanisms (Voas and Rebay, 2004; Scheres, 2007; Han et al., 2014; Sozzani and Iyer-Pascuzzi, 2014; Sablowski, 2015; Tuazon and Mullins, 2015; Fisher and Sozzani, 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge with citations.
